newsitem.title: UK: Power poised to return to Scotland, Wales.
newsitem.headline: Power poised to return to Scotland, Wales.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair, a man born and educated in Scotland, has lost no time in making good a key election promise by offering his native land a degree of independence through the ballot box.

He has proposed that a parliament with legislative and limited tax-raising powers in Edinburgh, and a more circumscribed body in Cardiff, should start to administer Scottish and Welsh internal affairs from 2000.

The plans will be subject to September referenda in the two countries. Few observers doubt there will be a huge "Yes" vote in Scotland, home to five million of Britain's 60 million population, but the result among the three million inhabitants of Wales is expected to be closer.
Blair's plan raised the hackles of right-wing politicians and newspapers backing the opposition Conservatives, who are wary of any weakening of the union of the countries that make up Britain.

A Daily Telegraph cartoon showed Blair, Scottish Secretary Donald Dewar and Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, also a Scot, slithering down a St Andrew's flag, symbol of Scotland, from a corner marked "devolution" towards one called "independence".
"Feed the tiger of Scottish nationalism on the meat of greater status and power, and it will not turn into a vegetarian," the paper warned in an editorial.
Blair has set his face determinedly against the break-up of Britain.

But his Labour Party, once sceptical that Britain's ramshackle constitution required reform, is now fully committed to devolution, the idea that power should flow away from central government in London to the constituent parts of Britain.
The idea of devolution -- although not the word -- has been around for more than a century in British politics.
Radicals pressed demands for "Home Rule All Round" -- separate parliaments for England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland -- with some success on Victorian Prime Minister William Gladstone.
In recent years, nationalists have emerged as a serious force in Scotland. The Scottish National Party (SNP) won 22 percent of the vote and six of the 72 Scottish seats at the May 1 British election.
Plaid Cymru, the SNP's Welsh equivalent, won 9.9 percent of the vote and four of the 40 seats. It is strong in areas where the country's ancient Celtic tongue is still widely spoken.

By contrast, the Conservatives, the only mainstream party which campaigned against Scottish and Welsh parliaments at the election, failed to win a single seat in either country, and did worse than the SNP in terms of votes.

Scotland lost its parliament with the Act of Union uniting its throne with that of England in 1707. Wales only ever had one national assembly, called by Owen Glendower early in the 15th century at the height of his rebellion against English rule.

By contrast, Northern Ireland was administered from the Protestant-dominated Stormont parliament building between 1921 and 1972, when the British government dissolved it, judging it was harming efforts to bring peace to the province.
Advocates of devolution see the Stormont example as irrelevant, and point instead to the success of "devolution" in other European countries, such as Spain, or of full-scale federalism in Germany.
But opponents say giving the Scots and Welsh power to administer their own affairs, but leaving England to be run by the British parliament, is a recipe for conflict.
Why should Scottish MPs be able to vote on English housing or social security policy when English MPs will have no voice on the same subjects in Scotland, they ask.
"The proposals strike at the most important principle of this country of ours -- the equality of our votes," said Conservative member of parliament Richard Shepherd.
Blair's government replies that it is willing to consider assemblies for the English regions if evidence can be shown for a substantial demand for them.
People in Cornwall, in the far south-west of England, recently marched on London to demand more say in their own affairs and more central government funding.
Such evidence is likely to manifest itself only if Scottish and Welsh parliaments prove more adept at attracting industry and investment than non-elected bodies in the English regions.

As for Northern Ireland, Stormont is likely to be revived only if relations between Catholics and Protestants in the province become much more friendly than they have been in the 76 years of the province's existence.
